_meta: A RoPE configuration -- the rotary base, the head dimension, the training context length, and a longer target context length -- used to show why extending a model's context should interpolate positions (scale them down into the trained range) rather than extrapolate them (feed positions larger than any seen in training). RoPE encodes position by rotating each pair of query/key dimensions by an angle proportional to the token's position, with a spectrum of frequencies: high-frequency pairs rotate a lot per position (they resolve nearby tokens), low-frequency pairs rotate very little per position (they carry long-range order). The dot product that attention computes then depends on the relative rotation between two positions, so what a trained model has actually seen is the set of rotation angles produced by positions and distances up to its training length L. Run the same model on a context longer than L and, for the low-frequency dimensions especially, the rotation angle at the far positions exceeds anything the model was trained on -- it is out of distribution, and attention degrades. Position interpolation fixes this by multiplying every position by L/target before applying RoPE, which squeezes the target-length range of positions back into the trained angle range, so no dimension ever rotates past an angle it saw in training. The cost is resolution: adjacent tokens are now closer in angle, so the model must distinguish positions it previously kept farther apart. base is the rotary base (frequency spacing), head_dim the per-head dimension (number of rotated coordinates), train_len the context length the model was trained on, target_len the longer context to run. These are the fixture; the frequency spectrum, the maximum rotation angles under training, extrapolation, and interpolation, and the resolution cost are computed.
